item.title: Microsoft Device Code Phishing, QuimaRAT MaaS, TrojPix, Opera GX, and SkillCloak
item.content:encoded:
When checking the URL isn’t enough: a Device Code Phishing attack via a Microsoft website — Should Read

Attackers are abusing Microsoft’s legitimate Device Code Flow to trick users into entering one-time codes on official Microsoft pages, allowing them to obtain access and refresh tokens even when MFA is completed. Organizations should disable Device Code Flow where unnecessary and monitor DeviceCodeSignIn events for anomalous activity.

  • The article describes a Device Code Phishing campaign in which attackers instructed victims to enter a one-time code on Microsoft’s legitimate device login page as part of the OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization Grant flow.
  • In the observed campaign from early April to mid-May 2026, victims received phishing emails styled as law firm notices with password-protected PDF attachments that led them through redirects and CAPTCHA pages to a phishing page displaying a one-time code.
  • After victims entered the code and completed MFA on Microsoft’s official page, the attackers obtained access_token, refresh_token, and id_token values that enabled access to email, OneDrive files, and Teams conversations.
  • A later variant targeting users in Brazil used an email in Portuguese and a link through the legitimate Cacoo.com domain as an open redirect to the phishing infrastructure.
  • The article recommends that users avoid entering unexpected authorization codes and that enterprises consider disabling Device Code Flow if unnecessary, monitor DeviceCodeSignIn events, enforce device compliance, and alert on unusual sign-in behavior.

SkillCloak Lets Malicious AI Agent Skills Evade Static Scanners with Self-Extracting Packing — Should Read

Researchers found that malicious AI agent “skills” can evade static scanners at high rates using simple obfuscation and self-extracting payloads, while still running normally on tools like Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. The key takeaway is that teams should not trust scan badges alone and need runtime behavior monitoring, least-privilege access, and stricter vetting for agent extensions.

  • Researchers at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology found that scanners for malicious AI agent skills can be evaded by simple changes that leave the malicious skill functioning.
  • The SKILLCLOAK tool rewrites malicious skills either by altering scanner-triggering bytes or by using self-extracting packing that hides the payload in skipped directories such as .git/.
  • Across eight scanners and 1,613 malicious skills from ClawHub, the self-extracting packing method bypassed each scanner more than 90% of the time and bypassed most of them more than 99% of the time.
  • The researchers proposed SKILLDETONATE, a sandbox-based runtime checker that watches file access, writes, and data transfers, and caught 97% of attacks in controlled tests with a 2% false-positive rate.
  • The article says public marketplaces already contain malicious skills, including Bitdefender’s finding that roughly 17% of skills checked on one marketplace carried hidden malicious code and Koi Security’s count of 341 malicious skills in the ClawHavoc campaign.

New Java-Based QuimaRAT MaaS Built to Run on Windows, Linux, and macOS — Should Read

Researchers warn that QuimaRAT is a new Java-based malware-as-a-service platform targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS with modular plugins, persistence, credential theft, surveillance, and resilient C2 features. Its builder, loader, and dropper tools are designed to help operators package payloads and evade detection across multiple delivery scenarios.

  • Cybersecurity researchers have identified QuimaRAT, a Java-based remote access trojan advertised as malware-as-a-service and capable of targeting Windows, Linux, and macOS environments.
  • QuimaRAT is built with a modular architecture that supports encrypted plugins delivered, loaded, unloaded, and updated from its command-and-control infrastructure.
  • The Quima suite includes Quima Control, Quima Builder, Quima Loader, and Quima Dropper, with tools for generating payload formats and staging browser-based delivery flows.
  • QuimaRAT uses operating system-specific persistence methods, including Windows Registry Run keys and scheduled tasks, Linux .desktop autostart entries and crontab reboot tasks, and macOS LaunchAgent plist files.
  • The malware supports capabilities such as remote command execution, plugin delivery, credential theft, file transfer, clipboard manipulation, webcam surveillance, and fileless shellcode execution on Windows hosts.

Opera GX Flaw Let Malicious Sites Auto-Install Mods to Steal Data From Visited Pages — Should Read

Opera patched a critical Opera GX flaw that let malicious websites silently install GX Mods and use CSS to steal data, such as a signed-in user’s Gmail address, from pages the victim visited. Users should ensure they are on Opera GX version 130.0.5847.89 or later.

  • Researchers found a flaw in Opera GX that allowed a malicious website to silently install a GX Mod and use it to extract specific data from pages a victim visited.
  • In a proof of concept, the researchers reconstructed a signed-in user's full Gmail address from a single visit without requiring any click from the victim.
  • Opera patched the flaw in Opera GX version 130.0.5847.89 and said it found no evidence that the issue was exploited in the wild.
  • The attack worked because GX Mods could be downloaded and enabled automatically without an approval prompt, and their CSS could apply to every page the browser opened.
  • Opera's bug bounty team ultimately rated the issue P1, its top severity, and paid the maximum $5,000 award for a critical bug.

New TrojPix Attack Leaks Data From Air-Gapped Systems via Video Cable Emissions — May Read

Researchers demonstrated TrojPix, a covert channel that lets malware on an air-gapped computer leak data by subtly modulating screen pixels so video cables emit decodable radio signals. It is lab research, but its reported speed of up to 8.1 Mbps shows that once malware is present, air-gapped systems could potentially exfiltrate whole files quickly unless protected with physical shielding, fiber links, and strong malware prevention.

  • Researchers at Shandong University demonstrated TrojPix, a technique that leaks data from air-gapped computers by subtly modifying on-screen pixels so video cables radiate a radio signal that a nearby receiver can decode.
  • TrojPix requires malware to already be present on the target machine and is a data exfiltration method rather than an initial access technique.
  • In tests, TrojPix reached a peak throughput of 8.1 Mbps and a maximum distance of 208 meters, with those measurements taken separately.
  • The researchers say TrojPix needs no administrator rights or hardware changes, and user-level malware that can draw to the screen is sufficient.
  • Suggested countermeasures include using fiber-optic video links instead of copper, shielding cables and rooms where needed, and preventing malware from getting onto the machine.
